items.answer: Photosynthesis

items.answer: (a) 420 kJ (b) 14% (c) plant cell walls contain cellulose, which is difficult to digest, so much remains undigested.

items.answer: (a) Habitat destruction; hunting / poaching; pollution; introduced species; climate change. (c) Maintain biodiversity and food webs; possible medicines; ecosystem services; ethical / cultural reasons.

items.answer: (a) Same student; temperature of the room. (b) 36.5 breaths/min (c) A line graph: time running on the x-axis and mean breathing rate on the y-axis.

items.stem: A food company in Cape Town uses three enzymes: pectinase for apple juice, lactase for milk, and proteases and lipases in its own laundry for staff uniforms. (a) Explain why pectinase increases the yield of apple juice. (b) Explain why lactose-free milk is useful for some people. (c) Explain why the laundry uses biological washing powder at 40 °C rather than 90 °C. (d) Suggest why enzymes used in industry are often obtained from microorganisms.
items.answer: (a) Pectin in cell walls is broken down, so cells break apart and release more juice. (b) People with lactose intolerance lack lactase, so lactose in milk causes digestive problems; in treated milk it has already been broken down. (c) Enzymes work well at 40 °C (near optimum), saving energy; at 90 °C they would be denatured. (d) Microorganisms grow rapidly in fermenters, producing large quantities of enzyme cheaply.

items.stem: A scientist studies cell division in a fruit fly, which has 8 chromosomes in each body cell. (a) Explain the importance of meiosis in sexual reproduction. (b) State where meiosis happens in a flowering plant and in a mammal. (c) Describe the role of stem cells.
items.answer: (a) Halves chromosome number so the zygote is diploid; produces variation in gametes. (b) Plant: anthers and ovules / ovaries. Mammal: testes and ovaries. (c) Unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis and can become specialised to replace or repair tissues.

items.stem: A cell in the human body produces keratin. The gene for this protein is on one of the chromosomes in the nucleus. (a) Describe how the information in the gene is used to make the protein. (b) Explain why the order of amino acids is important.
items.answer: (a) Gene is copied into mRNA in the nucleus; mRNA passes to a ribosome in the cytoplasm; ribosome reads the base sequence in triplets and joins amino acids in that order. (b) It determines how the protein folds and its shape, so whether it can carry out its function.

items.stem: Concentrations (g per 100 cm³) in blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine: protein: plasma 8.0, filtrate 0, urine 0; glucose: plasma 0.1, filtrate 0.1, urine 0; salts: plasma 0.72, filtrate 0.72, urine 1.5. For each substance, explain the differences between the three values.
items.answer: protein: too large to be filtered, so absent from filtrate and urine; glucose: filtered but all reabsorbed, so absent from urine; salts: filtered; some reabsorbed, excess excreted; more concentrated in urine as water is reabsorbed
items.markingKey: protein [2]; glucose [2]; salts [2] [6]

items.stem: In a population of rabbits, some individuals have thicker fur. During a period of very cold winters, the proportion of rabbits with thicker fur increased over several generations. (a) Explain how the proportion of rabbits with thicker fur increased, using the theory of natural selection. (b) Explain why the change takes several generations. (c) Suggest what would happen if the environment changed back.
items.answer: (a) Variation exists (from mutation); individuals with thicker fur are better adapted, so more survive very cold winters and reproduce, passing on the alleles; over generations the allele frequency increases. (b) Allele frequencies change only when individuals reproduce; each generation increases the proportion a little. (c) Thicker fur would no longer give an advantage, so the frequency of the allele may stay the same, or fall if the feature has a cost.
items.markingKey: (a) variation [1]; better adapted survive [1]; reproduce [1]; pass on alleles [1] [4] (b) [2] (c) [2]

(a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean distance fallen after 15 practice attempts, ignoring any anomalous result. (c) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Same hand used; same starting position of fingers. (b) 10.25 cm (c) As the number of practice attempts increases, the distance fallen decreases (reaction time gets shorter), levelling off.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: same hand used; same starting position of fingers; same person dropping the ruler; no warning before the drop; same ruler [2] (b) (10 + 10.5) ÷ 2 [1] = 10.25 cm [1] [2] (c) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) 190.6 g per week (b) 170%

items.stem: A farmer in Madrid grows maize in a field that sometimes becomes waterlogged. In alternate years she grows clover (a legume) and ploughs it into the soil. (a) Explain how growing and ploughing in clover increases the nitrate in the soil. (b) Describe how nitrate ions are absorbed by the roots.
items.answer: (a) Clover has root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which convert nitrogen gas to ammonium; when ploughed in, decomposers release ammonium, which nitrifying bacteria convert to nitrate. (b) By active transport into root hair cells, using energy from respiration, against a concentration gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) nitrogen-fixing bacteria in nodules [1]; decomposition [1]; nitrification [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Satellite images show the forest area in the Congo basin fell from 650 thousand km² in 1995 to 498 thousand km² in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Calculate the mean rate of loss per year. (c) Assuming this rate continues, calculate how many more years it would take for all the forest to be lost. (d) State two consequences of this deforestation.
items.answer: (a) 23.4% (b) 7.6 thousand km² per year (c) 66 years (d) loss of habitats / extinction; soil erosion; flooding; increased CO₂.

items.stem: In a region near Santiago, most farmers grow the same variety of sugar cane, propagated asexually from cuttings. A new fungal disease has started to spread. (a) Explain why asexual propagation is popular with farmers. (b) Explain why the new disease is a serious threat. (c) Suggest how scientists could use sexual reproduction to help.
items.answer: (a) Quick; offspring identical, so they keep high yield and quality; no pollination needed. (b) All plants are genetically identical so none has resistance; disease can spread through the whole crop. (c) Cross-breed varieties to produce varied offspring and select those resistant to the disease.

items.stem: A doctor in Riyadh compares lung tissue from a non-smoker and a long-term smoker with emphysema. The total alveolar surface area is about 75 m² in the non-smoker and 43 m² in the smoker. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in surface area. (b) Explain why the smoker becomes breathless during mild exercise. (c) Name two other components of tobacco smoke and state their effects.
items.answer: (a) 42.7% (b) Smaller surface area means less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so less is available for aerobic respiration in muscles. (c) Nicotine: addictive, raises heart rate; carbon monoxide: combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport; tar: carcinogen.
items.markingKey: (a) (75 − 43) ÷ 75 × 100 [1] = 42.7% [1] [2] (b) less diffusion [1]; less oxygen for respiration [1] [2] (c) two components with effects [2]

items.stem: A maize body cell contains 20 chromosomes. State how many chromosomes are found in (a) a gamete, (b) a zygote, (c) a cell produced by mitosis of a skin cell, and (d) the number of pairs of chromosomes in a body cell.

A bodybuilder in Seoul eats a diet very high in protein shakes. A urine test shows high urea concentration. (a) Describe the route taken by urea from where it is made to where it leaves the body. (b) Suggest why the bodybuilder is advised to drink more water. (c) Explain why the body needs some amino acids every day.
items.answer: (a) Liver → hepatic vein → blood → renal artery → kidney (filtered) → ureter → bladder → urethra. (b) More water is needed to dissolve and excrete the extra urea in urine. (c) To make new proteins for growth, repair, enzymes and antibodies.

items.stem: Breeders in Colombo selected cows with the highest milk yield for 5 generations. The mean milk yield rose from 4000 to 6855 L per lactation. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean increase per generation. (c) Describe the procedure the breeders used.
items.answer: (a) 71.4% (b) 571 L per lactation per generation (c) selected individuals with the highest milk yield, bred them, selected the best offspring and repeated each generation.

items.stem: An optometrist in Seoul tests a patient's vision. The patient reads a chart 6 m away and then a card held 25 cm from the eyes. (a) Explain why the optometrist dims the lights before examining the retina. (b) State where light should be focused for the sharpest colour image and why. (c) Explain how information from the retina reaches the brain.
items.answer: (a) In dim light the pupil dilates (radial muscles contract), so more of the retina can be seen. (b) On the fovea, which has the most cones. (c) Rods and cones generate impulses carried along sensory neurones in the optic nerve to the brain.

items.stem: A graph shows the concentrations of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the blood during a 28-day menstrual cycle in which no pregnancy occurs. (a) Describe the changes in progesterone concentration during the cycle and explain their effect. (b) Explain why FSH concentration is high at the start of the cycle. (c) Explain why oestrogen concentration rises between day 5 and day 13.
items.answer: (a) Low in first half; rises after ovulation (from corpus luteum) to a peak around day 21; falls before day 28, causing menstruation. (b) To stimulate a follicle in the ovary to mature an egg and produce oestrogen. (c) The developing follicle secretes oestrogen, which repairs and thickens the uterus lining.

items.answer: (a) Habitat destruction; hunting / poaching; pollution; introduced species; climate change. items.stem: Mateo filled identical test tubes with water at 70 °C, wrapped them in different numbers of layers of cotton wool (as a model of fat or fur insulation) and measured the temperature drop over 10 minutes. (d) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Trial 3 with 1 layers (8.6 °C); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) 13.85 °C (c) More layers trap more air, a poor conductor, so less heat is lost by conduction and convection; this models how fat and fur reduce heat loss in animals. (d) Use a lid on each tube to reduce heat loss from the top.

items.answer: (a) 86.7% (b) Not enough pollen grains landed / some pollen tubes did not reach ovules, so some ovules were not fertilised. (c) The fruit. (d) Water, oxygen, suitable temperature; e.g. oxygen for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth.

items.stem: Sofia accidentally touches a cactus spine in a garden in Santiago and pulls the hand away before feeling any pain. (a) Describe the pathway of the nerve impulse. (b) Explain why the pain is felt after the hand has moved. (c) Describe how an impulse passes across a synapse.
items.answer: (a) Pain receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in spinal cord → motor neurone → muscle in arm (effector). (b) The impulse also travels up the spinal cord to the brain, a longer pathway; conscious awareness takes longer than the reflex. (c) Neurotransmitter released from vesicles, diffuses across the gap, binds to receptors on next neurone.

items.stem: A group of students in Auckland grew maize plants from seeds of the same variety. Half were grown in fertile soil in full sun and half in poor soil in shade. (b) Explain why plants grown from the same variety still showed a range of heights within each group. (c) Name one feature of these plants likely to show discontinuous variation and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Continuous variation; histogram. (b) Genetic differences between seeds (alleles from sexual reproduction) and small differences in local environment. (c) Flower colour (or seed colour): controlled by one or a few genes, giving distinct categories.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) genetic variation [1]; environmental variation [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.answer: (a) 120 kJ (b) 6% (c) plant cell walls contain cellulose, which is difficult to digest, so much remains undigested.

items.stem: A hospital in Kuala Lumpur records the blood groups of a family. The mother is group A, the father is group B, and their first child is group O. (a) Deduce the genotypes of the parents, explaining your answer. (b) State the probability that the next child will be blood group AB. (c) Explain why blood group is an example of discontinuous variation.
items.answer: (a) Mother IAIo and father IBIo, because the child (IoIo) must have received Io from each parent. (b) 25% (1 in 4). (c) There are a few distinct categories (A, B, AB, O) with no intermediates; controlled by genes only.

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains 16.7% oxygen and 3.8% carbon dioxide. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen. (b) Calculate how many times greater the carbon dioxide concentration is in exhaled air. (c) Explain these changes.
items.answer: (a) 20.5% (b) 95 times (c) Oxygen diffuses into the blood and is used in respiration; carbon dioxide from respiration diffuses into the alveoli.

items.stem: In a region of tropical rainforest, large areas are being cleared for timber. Scientists report fewer species in the remaining forest, more frequent floods, and a fall in local rainfall. (a) Explain why local rainfall has fallen. (b) Explain why floods have become more frequent. (c) Suggest two ways of reducing the impact of deforestation.
items.answer: (a) Fewer trees means less transpiration, so less water vapour enters the atmosphere to form clouds. (b) Without roots and leaf litter, rain runs off quickly; eroded soil silts up rivers. (c) Replant trees (reforestation); sustainable logging; protected areas; laws and education; buying certified products.

items.stem: A bodybuilder in Karachi eats a diet very high in protein shakes. A urine test shows high urea concentration. (a) Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the body. (b) Describe the route taken by urea from where it is made to where it leaves the body. (c) Explain why the body needs some amino acids every day.
items.answer: (a) They are deaminated in the liver; the nitrogen-containing part is converted to urea; the rest is used for respiration or stored as glycogen/fat. (b) Liver → hepatic vein → blood → renal artery → kidney (filtered) → ureter → bladder → urethra. (c) To make new proteins for growth, repair, enzymes and antibodies.

items.stem: In a country, new HIV infections fell from 65 559 in 2008 to 28 977 in 2018. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Suggest two measures that could have caused this decrease.
items.answer: (a) 55.8% (b) e.g. condom distribution, education, needle exchange schemes, blood screening, antiviral drugs for pregnant women.

items.stem: A food company in Kathmandu uses three enzymes: pectinase for apple juice, lactase for milk, and proteases and lipases in its own laundry for staff uniforms. (a) Explain why pectinase increases the yield of apple juice. (b) Explain why lactose-free milk is useful for some people. (c) Name the substances produced when lipase digests a grease stain.
items.answer: (a) Pectin in cell walls is broken down, so cells break apart and release more juice. (b) People with lactose intolerance lack lactase, so lactose in milk causes digestive problems; in treated milk it has already been broken down. (c) Fatty acids and glycerol.

items.stem: Tomás grew cress seedlings in boxes with a hole on one side, and measured the angle of bending of the shoots towards the light after 3 days at different distances from a lamp. items.answer: (a) 27.5 ° (b) With brighter light (closer lamp) the difference in light between the two sides is greater; more auxin moves to the shaded side, causing more cell elongation there and greater bending.

items.stem: Marram grass grows on coastal sand dunes near Liverpool. The sand drains quickly and the dunes are exposed to strong, dry winds. In dry weather its leaves roll up, with the stomata on the inner surface among many hairs. (a) State the term for a plant adapted to dry conditions. (b) Explain why reducing water loss also reduces the rate of photosynthesis. (c) Compare the adaptations of marram grass with those of a water lily.
items.answer: (a) Xerophyte. (b) Closing or enclosing stomata reduces diffusion of carbon dioxide into the leaf, so less CO₂ for photosynthesis. (c) Marram: thick cuticle, few sunken stomata on inner surface, rolled leaves; water lily: thin cuticle, stomata on upper surface, air spaces, large floating leaves.

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates breathing using a bell jar model: balloons attached to a Y-tube represent the lungs, the bell jar represents the thorax, and a rubber sheet at the bottom represents the diaphragm. (a) State one way in which the model is not like the real thorax. (b) Describe the role of the intercostal muscles during inhalation. (c) Explain why pressure changes cause air to move. (d) Describe how forced exhalation differs from exhalation at rest.
items.answer: (a) It has no ribs or intercostal muscles; the walls cannot move; the diaphragm is pulled, not contracted; balloons are not alveoli. (b) External intercostals contract, moving the ribcage up and out, increasing thorax volume. (c) Air moves from a region of higher pressure to lower pressure. (d) At rest exhalation is passive (muscles relax); in forced exhalation the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles contract to push air out.

items.stem: A bodybuilder in Dhaka eats a diet very high in protein shakes. A urine test shows high urea concentration. (a) Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the body. (b) Describe the route taken by urea from where it is made to where it leaves the body. (c) Suggest why the bodybuilder is advised to drink more water. items.answer: (a) They are deaminated in the liver; the nitrogen-containing part is converted to urea; the rest is used for respiration or stored as glycogen/fat. items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in a rocky seashore. items.answer: (a) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. items.stem: In a country, new HIV infections fell from 68 439 in 2010 to 27 868 in 2020. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Suggest two measures that could have caused this decrease.

items.stem: A student compares flowers of orchid (insect-pollinated) and maize (wind-pollinated). (a) Describe two features you would expect to see in the orchid flower. (b) Explain how the stigma of the maize flower is adapted. (c) Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination. (d) Describe what happens after a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma.
items.answer: (a) large, brightly coloured petals; scent and nectar. (b) large feathery stigmas outside the flower— catches pollen from the air. items.stem: Students studied feeding relationships in an African savanna. items.answer: (a) grass (1) → grasshoppers (2) → lizards (3) → birds (4) (b) Energy is lost at each level (about 90%), so too little energy remains to support further levels. (c) They break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide and mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) for producers.

items.answer: (a) Habitat destruction; hunting / poaching; pollution; introduced species; climate change. items.answer: (a) Select plants with the most grain; breed them; choose offspring with the greatest grain yield; repeat over many generations. (b) Humans choose vs environment; features useful to humans vs features aiding survival; faster vs slower.

items.answer: (a) 3.3 (b) Use more quadrats (and calculate the mean). (c) Daisies do not move (or move very slowly), so they are not counted twice or missed.

items.answer: (a) 37.8 times (b) In A, roots and leaf litter hold water and soil; trees take up and transpire water; B has no roots so water runs off. (c) Soil washes into rivers, raising the river bed so it overflows more easily.

items.stem: A cell in the human body produces haemoglobin. The gene for this protein is on one of the chromosomes in the nucleus. (a) Describe how the information in the gene is used to make the protein. (b) Explain why a mutation in the gene could prevent the protein working.

items.answer: (a) Quick; offspring identical, so they keep high yield and quality; no pollination needed. (b) All plants are genetically identical so none has resistance; disease can spread through the whole crop. (c) Cross-breed varieties to produce varied offspring and select those resistant to the disease.

items.stem: Felix filled identical test tubes with water at 70 °C, wrapped them in different numbers of layers of cotton wool (as a model of fat or fur insulation) and measured the temperature drop over 10 minutes. Results table. Number of layers of insulation: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Temperature drop / °C, trial 1: 25.4, 9.4, 10.8, 8.5, 7.1; trial 2: 25.1, 15.1, 10.3, 8, 7.1; trial 3: 23.7, 14.9, 10.1, 8.5, 7.1. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 with 1 layers (9.4 °C); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) As the number of layers of insulation increases, the temperature drop decreases and then levels off at about 3 layers.

items.stem: A doctor in Dubai compares lung tissue from a non-smoker and a long-term smoker with emphysema. The total alveolar surface area is about 75 m² in the non-smoker and 27 m² in the smoker. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in surface area. (b) Explain why the smoker becomes breathless during mild exercise. (c) Describe how the cilia and mucus normally protect the lungs, and how smoking affects them.
items.answer: (a) 64% (b) Smaller surface area means less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so less is available for aerobic respiration in muscles. (c) Mucus traps pathogens and dust; cilia sweep it up and out. Smoke paralyses / destroys cilia, so mucus builds up, causing coughing and infections.
items.markingKey: (a) (75 − 27) ÷ 75 × 100 [1] = 64% [1] [2] (b) less diffusion [1]; less oxygen for respiration [1] [2] (c) normal function [1]; effect of smoking [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2. Number of fronds, trial 1: 14, 30, 41, 51, 59; trial 2: 14, 31, 60, 50, 60; trial 3: 14, 31, 39, 51, 57. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) Independent: concentration of fertiliser; dependent: number of fronds. (b) Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins for growth, so more fronds are produced; at high concentrations another factor (e.g. light, space) becomes limiting, so the increase levels off.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = concentration of fertiliser [1]; dependent variable = number of fronds [1] [2] (b) nitrate for proteins / growth [1]; more growth / fronds [1]; another limiting factor [1] [3]

items.stem: Elena measured reaction time by catching a falling ruler. The distance the ruler fell before being caught was recorded for five attempts each after different numbers of practice attempts. Results table. Number of practice attempts: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. Distance fallen / cm, trial 1: 12.9, 15.9, 13, 10.9, 9.9; trial 2: 20.4, 16, 12.6, 10.6, 10.1; trial 3: 20.8, 15.1, 11.9, 10.8, 9.4. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Calculate the reaction time for the first set of results using t = √(2d ÷ 9.8), with d in metres. (c) Explain why catching the ruler is not a reflex action.
items.answer: (a) Independent: number of practice attempts; dependent: distance fallen. (b) 0.205 s (c) It involves conscious thought / the brain making a decision, and it is learned rather than automatic.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = number of practice attempts [1]; dependent variable = distance fallen [1] [2] (b) d = 0.206 m [1]; t = √(2 × 0.206 ÷ 9.8) = 0.205 s [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: A scientist studies cell division in a pea, which has 14 chromosomes in each body cell. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a cell produced by mitosis and in a cell produced by meiosis. (b) Explain why the cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical. (c) Explain the importance of meiosis in sexual reproduction.
items.answer: (a) mitosis 14; meiosis 7 (b) Chromosomes are copied exactly before division and one copy of each goes into each new cell. (c) Halves chromosome number so the zygote is diploid; produces variation in gametes.

items.stem: State the function of each structure: (i) scrotum, (ii) oviduct, (iii) urethra.
items.answer: (i) holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature (ii) carries the egg to the uterus; site of fertilisation (iii) carries semen (or urine) out of the body through the penis

items.stem: Tomás estimated the population of clover plants on a school field in Lagos measuring 20 m × 30 m. 10 quadrats, each 1 m², were placed at random. Number of clover plants in each quadrat: 14, 12, 9, 12, 16, 14, 10, 10, 13, 16. (a) Suggest how the estimate could be made more reliable. (b) Suggest one environmental factor that could affect the distribution of clover plants and how it could be measured. (c) Suggest why counting clover plants is easier with quadrats than counting animals such as beetles.
items.answer: (a) Use more quadrats (and calculate the mean). (b) Light intensity (light meter); soil moisture or pH (meter / probe); trampling. (c) Clover plants do not move (or move very slowly), so they are not counted twice or missed.

items.stem: Isla added pectinase to 50 g samples of chopped apple at different temperatures, left them for 15 minutes, then filtered each for 10 minutes and measured the volume of juice collected. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55. Volume of juice / cm³, trial 1: 6.2, 9.2, 19.7, 16, 20.2; trial 2: 6.3, 9.8, 19.3, 28, 19.1; trial 3: 6.4, 9.2, 20.2, 26.6, 20. (a) Explain the results. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Pectinase breaks down pectin in cell walls, releasing juice; up to about 45 °C more kinetic energy gives more enzyme–substrate collisions; above the optimum the enzyme is denatured and the active site changes shape. (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean volume of juice on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) pectin broken down [1]; more collisions to optimum [1]; denaturation [1] [3] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and volume of juice on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 14, 17, 17, 18; trial 2: 6, 14, 17, 18, 18; trial 3: 3, 14, 16, 17, 18. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) As the concentration of antibiotic increases, the diameter of clear zone increases and then levels off at about 30 µg/cm³. (b) Antibiotic diffuses out from the disc into the agar and kills bacteria; a higher concentration gives a steeper gradient and reaches killing concentration further from the disc, so the clear zone is wider.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) diffusion from disc [1]; bacteria killed [1]; higher concentration diffuses further [1] [3]

items.stem: A student compares flowers of grass (wind-pollinated) and hibiscus (insect-pollinated). (a) Describe two features you would expect to see in the grass flower. (b) Explain how the stigma of the hibiscus flower is adapted. (c) Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
items.answer: (a) small, dull or no petals; no scent or nectar. (b) stigma inside the flower, sticky— pollen sticks to it when insects brush past. (c) Self: pollen to stigma of same flower / same plant. Cross: pollen to stigma of a different plant of the same species.

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Toronto has been very thirsty, tired and losing weight. A test shows glucose in the urine and high blood glucose. The doctor diagnoses type 1 diabetes. (a) Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated. (b) Describe the role of glucagon when blood glucose falls during exercise. (c) Explain why the child is losing weight.
items.answer: (a) Regular insulin injections (or pump), monitoring blood glucose, controlling carbohydrate intake and exercise. (b) Pancreas secretes glucagon; liver breaks glycogen down to glucose, raising blood glucose. (c) Without insulin cells cannot take up and use glucose well, so fat and protein are respired instead.

items.stem: Felix mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 8, 29, 39, 16, 2; trial 2: 8, 31, 37, 16, 3; trial 3: 8, 30, 36, 16, 2. (a) Calculate the mean number of bubbles at 60 °C, ignoring any anomalous result. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: (a) 2 bubbles in 2 min (b) Use boiled yeast with sugar solution; no bubbles should be produced, showing that living yeast causes the gas production.
